appraisal_events.evidence: 'Un homme au menton et aux lèvres rasés, aux favoris de maître d'hôtel, débitant sur un ton de condescendance des plaisanteries de professeur de seconde... et c'est Brichot'; at Verdurin's naming him, 'il n'a pas une parole qui marque qu'il connaisse nos livres.'
appraisal_events.explanation: Brichot is given an unflattering portrait — a maître d'hôtel's whiskers, condescending schoolmasterly jokes — and further deflated by failing to acknowledge the diarist's work when introduced.

appraisal_events.evidence: 'C'est moi qui lui ai fait connaître tout cela... Les fleurs, il n'en avait jamais vu, il ne savait pas distinguer un althéa d'une passe-rose. C'est moi qui lui ai appris à reconnaître... le jasmin... On ne l'appelait chez nous que Monsieur Tiche... s'il n'avait pas fait ce sale mariage!'
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme Verdurin claims personal credit for Elstir's celebrated skill at painting flowers and composing portraits, reframing his gift as her tutelage and voicing bitter resentment at the marriage that took him from her circle.

appraisal_events.evidence: Swann identifies the pearls' 'portrait authentique, dans la collection du duc de Guermantes,' proclaiming it 'une collection qui n'a pas son égale au monde... devant les exclamations des convives un brin ébahis.'
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann displays authoritative connoisseurship about the pearls and the Guermantes collection, visibly impressing the assembled guests.

appraisal_events.evidence: 'Le docteur Cottard, avec une finesse qui décèle chez lui l'homme tout à fait distingué'... cites the case 'd'une façon vraiment plus philosophique que ne feraient bien des médecins'; later, 'Cottard, qui se révèle un curieux vraiment pénétrant en toutes choses.'
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator credits Cottard with unexpected finesse and penetrating insight in his psychological analysis of the fire and the altered valet, elevating him above his usual comic register.

status_effects.explanation: The unflattering physical description and pedantic, dismissive manner lower Brichot's local standing in the narrator's portrait.
His signature artistic gift is recast as something taught and directed by Mme Verdurin rather than innate, and he is spoken of with proprietary resentment.
Before the assembled dinner guests, she asserts that she personally made the now-celebrated Elstir the painter he became, a claim that inflates her own standing by association with his fame.
His confident, expert intervention about the pearls' provenance visibly astonishes the other guests.
The narrator explicitly names Cottard's finesse and penetrating insight, elevating him above his usual comic treatment.

ambiguities: Mme Verdurin's claim of having taught Elstir is voiced within a pastiche of the Goncourt journal whose reliability the surrounding chapter later calls into question (the narrator recalls finding these same people 'insipide' and 'commun' in retrospect); this passage alone does not clearly signal irony, so endorsement of her claim is left uncertain.
